Real-time streaming pipeline

A shift opens up at a warehouse, and somebody needs to know. In the old setup the dashboard that should show it caught up once an hour, when a batch job ran. This repo is the streaming pipeline I built to replace that job, during my summer 2025 data engineering internship at Amazon. With it, an event is searchable less than a second after it reaches the pipeline.

It reads shift-opportunity events from an SNS topic in the Sydney region, carries them to a Kinesis stream in N. Virginia, transforms them in an Apache Flink job, and writes three views of the data to OpenSearch.

Result

  • 600–900 ms end to end, from SNS to a searchable OpenSearch document. The target was 120 seconds.
  • The upstream service took another 5–10 seconds to publish each event. Nothing in this pipeline can change that part.
  • The Lambda stage has headroom for 300K+ events a minute. That is a capacity estimate, not traffic it carried.
  • Other teams later reused the design for their own real-time work.

How it works

 upstream service ── SNS topic (Sydney)
                          │  cross-region subscription
                          ▼
                 Lambda processor (N. Virginia) ──── fails ───► dead-letter queue
                 validates, enriches, retries                         │
                          │                                           │ replay
                          │ ◄─────────────────────────────────────────┘
                          │ ◄──── replay ──── S3 archive of raw events (filled outside this repo)
                          ▼
                 Kinesis Data Stream
                          │
                          ▼
                 Flink job (Java DataStream API)
                    ├──► OpenSearch: current state   upsert, older updates ignored
                    ├──► OpenSearch: event log       append only
                    ├──► OpenSearch: per associate   one document per assigned worker, upsert and delete
                    └──► S3 (optional copy of the log)
                          │
                          ▼
                 OpenSearch Dashboards

Each event is deeply nested JSON. The Flink job flattens it, works out a status, notes which fields changed, and sends it to three indexes that answer different questions:

Index Write pattern Question it answers
current state upsert, one document per opportunity What does this shift look like right now?
event log append only What happened, and in what order?
per associate upsert and delete, one document per worker Who is on which shift?

Events can arrive out of order. By default each update goes to OpenSearch with a short Painless script that compares timestamps there and keeps the stored document if it is newer. That gives exactly-once results without a read before every write. A faster mode skips the check for streams whose order is guaranteed. Counting both modes, the job wires five sink variants, and in production each one signs its requests with IAM (SigV4).

Failed records go to a dead-letter queue. The same Lambda can replay that queue into Kinesis, or re-read archived raw events from S3. Four CloudWatch alarms watch the error rate, both failure queues and the success rate.

Why Flink

I compared five designs before writing the job:

Design Latency Exactly-once Several sinks from one stream
SNS → Firehose → S3 → Lambda → OpenSearch minutes of buffering no no
SNS → Lambda → OpenSearch directly good no by hand
SNS → Lambda → Kinesis → Data Prepper → OpenSearch batch delays no limited
SNS → Lambda → Kinesis → OpenSearch Ingestion → OpenSearch moderate no no
SNS → Lambda → Kinesis → Flink → OpenSearch under a second yes yes

Flink cost the most at development scale. It was also the only design that could keep updates in order and write three differently shaped indexes from one stream.

What went wrong

I started in a Flink Studio notebook with PyFlink and SQL. One sink worked. The second one hung: the job looped on the first INSERT and never reached the next, and the docs confirmed that notebooks allow a single sink. I got several sinks running by editing the generated code so that every INSERT ran in one statement set.

Then I hit two limits I could not edit around. The Python Table API had no way to make an update conditional on a timestamp, and it only supported username and password auth, not IAM. I threw away more than three weeks of notebook work and rewrote the job in Java. The lesson I kept: check the auth and sink requirements against the runtime before building the prototype, not after.

What is in the repo

Path What it is
shift-opportunity-consumer-amazon-managed-service-for-apache-flink/ the Flink job (Java 11, Flink 1.20) with its own README and architecture notes
lambda-functions/unified-processor/ the Lambda that moves SNS events into Kinesis, plus the dead-letter and S3 replay modes
lambda-functions/ShiftOppSimulator-stack-DataSimulator.py a simulator that generates fake events for testing
cloudformation-templates/ stacks for the processor, the cross-region subscription and its dead-letter queue, and the simulator
iam-roles/ an export of the Flink application role
opensearch dashboards/ saved dashboards for the business view and system health
docs/ the design document I wrote for the project, and its challenges write-up

Running it

This was built for a company AWS environment. It is here to read, and it will not run as it stands: you need your own SNS topic, Kinesis stream and OpenSearch domain. ARNs in the docs and test files use arn:<partition>: and the example account 123456789012 as placeholders. The CloudFormation stacks that subscribe to the upstream topic take it as a required parameter.

To build the Flink job:

cd shift-opportunity-consumer-amazon-managed-service-for-apache-flink
mvn package

The Flink README and the processor README cover configuration.
